summary: Epsilon Indi B is a known pair of brown dwarfs that orbit the star Epsilon Indi, 12.1 light-years away. WANDERERS measured a 75-arcsecond move from 2010 to 2026, or 4.72 arcseconds per year. This is within 0.7% of the Gaia DR3 value of 4.68. The object is 2.4 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3 microns, which is the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf. Confidence is high because all three required checks passed. The brightness check did not pass (-0.01 ± 0.08 mag), and 59 of 149 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: It moved 75 arcseconds since 2010. Its speed is 4.72 arcseconds per year, within 0.7% of Gaia's 4.68, so it is the same object, about 12.1 light-years away. It is 2.4 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than in the 3.3 micron methane band. Methane makes that dip in cold brown dwarfs. But 59 of 149 spectrum points are flagged, and the steady-brightness check did not pass (-0.01 ± 0.08 mag).

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Three things would make me less sure. First, 59 of the 149 spectrum points are flagged, so much of the spectrum is uncertain. Second, the brightness check did not pass. The change of -0.01 magnitudes is small next to its ±0.08 uncertainty, so we cannot say that the brightness was steady. Third, this is a pair of brown dwarfs. SPHEREx probably sees them as one blended dot, so each measurement mixes their light.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE imaged this spot in 2010, and SPHEREx imaged it in 2025 and 2026. Over that 16-year gap, Epsilon Indi B moved 75 arcseconds, about 12 SPHEREx pixels. That gives a speed of 4.72 arcseconds per year, close to Gaia's 4.68. SPHEREx also splits the light into a spectrum, which shows a methane dip: 2.4 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3. Caution: 59 of 149 spectrum points are flagged.
